*   Understanding of arrays and nested loops in C/C++.

## Introduction & background

Self-capacitance works perfectly for single buttons, but scaling it to a full screen requires a dedicated trace for every single pixel, which is impossible to route. Mutual capacitance solves this by scanning a matrix of intersecting rows and columns. Instead of measuring capacitance to ground, you measure the capacitive coupling between a driven row and a sensing column. When a finger approaches the intersection, it steals some of the electric field lines, decreasing the mutual capacitance. However, primitive matrix scanning suffers from "ghosting," where pressing two diagonal points creates alternative current paths, tricking the controller into registering a third or fourth phantom touch.

## Core equations

$$C_{mutual} = \frac{\varepsilon A}{d}$$

## What you're building

1. A physical 2x2 multi-touch trackpad prototype utilizing a row/column copper foil grid.
2. Firmware to sequentially drive the rows and sense the columns using [Day 2](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-02.md)'s charge-transfer logic.
3. A filtering system using a 20-sample moving-average baseline and a fixed threshold to process the touches.

## Activity

Cut a 2×2 foil matrix. Drive rows with GPIOs, sense columns with [Day 2](https://hardware.ellietaghavi.com/llm/day-02.md)'s code. Add a 20-sample moving-average baseline and a fixed threshold. Localize a touch to a cell; record a demo.

## Question to answer

1. Physically, where do "ghost" touches appear when you press two diagonal cells at the same time?
2. Why does true mutual-capacitance scanning (driving one row and sensing columns per intersection) fix the ghosting problem that per-pad self-capacitance scanning cannot?
